lore.meridian_brewing.qi_gather:
Come, sit by the hearth. This old woman has kept her brewing pot in this muddy swamp her whole life; the moss underfoot has grown back more times than I can count. Since you have come to learn the craft, I will start with Qi Gathering Soup. It is the most important aid to breathing practice. The old folk always drank a bowl before sitting to meditate, for it lets your lungs draw in far more spirit qi while you breathe. But it is a fierce draught. Once you have taken your fill and the soup wears off, your lungs go weak for a while and you draw in only eight parts in ten. Brew it well, though, and that little strain is nothing.

Before you open a cauldron for this soup, hold the Qi Gathering Soup recipe up before your eyes and read it through. You must also find the brewing scroll and study it until the brewing technique is truly yours. Such things mostly sit in the hands of witches who have reached the True Qi realm, or lie in the chests of witch huts newly risen in the swamp. If you have not committed the recipe to memory and learned the stance, you may pile up herbs like a mountain and the cauldron still will not heed you.

For tools, start by hammering 7 copper ingots into a Copper Cauldron. It holds 3 portions of water and yields 2 bottles. Copper is precious: left under the open sky, wind and rain slowly rust it, and then it carries heat more slowly. Rub a coat of wax on it with a honeycomb to keep the rust off, and if it has rusted, scrape it clean with an axe, little by little. Once your hands are skilled, forge 1 Copper Cauldron and 3 iron ingots into a Witch Cauldron. It holds 2 portions of water, yields 1 bottle, and the heat moves through it faster.

This soup loves the sun, so it needs sun fire. A campfire under the cauldron is sun fire. You can also set the Witch Cauldron on an Iron Stove. A newly placed stove already burns sun fire; if it ever gets changed, press a handful of sand against the cauldron and it turns back to sun fire. The Iron Stove is a fine thing. It is cold when first placed. Touch the cauldron with coal or charcoal and the stove rises one level; tap it with a shovel and it drops one level. It has four heats: 75 degrees, 85 degrees, 93 degrees and 100 degrees, and it holds steady, wavering by only 1 degree. Each piece of coal you add stores 60 seconds of fuel. While that fuel lasts, the fire stays put at its level; only once it has burned out does it sink one level every 60 seconds by itself, so just make sure there is enough fuel before you begin. For this soup the heat must stay pinned between 86 and 94 degrees. Level 3 on the stove is exactly 93 degrees, which saves you all the worry. A campfire always clings close to 100 degrees, a good step hotter than this soup wants, and you cannot turn it down. While the cauldron is not full you can pour in a bottle of cold water to press it down: one portion of cold water cools a Copper Cauldron by 15 degrees and a Witch Cauldron by 10 degrees. But the campfire never rests, and before long it burns back up.

Now the ingredients. The main herb is Smoked Pufferfish: put a fresh pufferfish in a smoker for 5 seconds and take it out. Prepared herbs are strongest within 3 days; after 3 days their virtue fades day by day, and by the 9th day only six parts in ten remain. Raw pufferfish will not go into the cauldron; it must be smoked first. For the base, have one glowstone dust ready. Qi Gathering Soup is only for drinking, so never get greedy and add gunpowder; gunpowder simply will not go in. Besides that, keep two more things ready in your left hand: the accessory, a prismarine shard, and the catalyst, a nautilus shell.

When brewing, the order must never slip. Water first: one water bucket poured into the cauldron gives 3 portions, one water bottle gives 1. Once it is full, drop in the Smoked Pufferfish first; with the main herb in, the foundation of the brew is set. Then sprinkle in the glowstone dust. Do not rush to start the brew yet. First let the cauldron sit between 40 and 79 degrees and soak for a full 10 seconds, so the herbs open up and the foundation grows rich. If you use an Iron Stove, keep it at level 1 while soaking, for 75 degrees is just right; once the soak is done, add coal to raise the level, and start the brew when the heat has come up.

To start, hold a stick in your right hand, fix your eyes on the cauldron and cast the brewing technique. The brew lasts 30 seconds, and the cauldron draws on your qi: 6 for a Copper Cauldron, 7.8 for a Witch Cauldron, taken slowly over the 30 seconds. If the qi of heaven and earth around you falls short, it takes the rest from the meridians you have opened; if the two together cannot cover it, the brewing technique will not even begin. During these 30 seconds never let your feet stray more than 3 blocks from the heart of the cauldron, and keep your eyes fixed on the cauldron or the fire beneath it. Look away for a moment, wander off, or let both the surroundings and your own body run dry of qi midway, and the brew breaks on the spot. A broken brew is not a total loss: the herbs and the soaking you did stay in the cauldron. But the qi already drawn is not returned, and the heat and the timing must be counted from the start again. The prismarine shard and nautilus shell you already put in also stay in the cauldron, yet they cannot be added a second time, so whatever precision they had is lost. You can only begin the brew anew.

Count the seconds and drop the herbs in with your left hand: between the 8th and 12th second, add the prismarine shard; between the 22nd and 26th second, add the nautilus shell. Those seconds are the surest. If your hand is a little slow or quick, within 4 seconds it will still do, with somewhat weaker virtue; any further off and the herb is all but wasted. If you never add the catalyst, you will never in your life brew a Superior soup. Keep the corner of your eye on the heat too: this soup will not scorch if the fire runs high, but once the heat leaves 86 to 94 degrees its virtue will not brew in fully. And above 90 degrees, a portion of water boils off for nothing every 20 seconds; when the water runs low and boils dry, the pot scorches through and everything is ruined.

When the full 30 seconds are done and the cauldron goes quiet, do not hurry to scoop with a bottle. The fire below will not rest on its own. With an Iron Stove, rake it a few times through the cauldron with a shovel to bring it down to level 1, 75 degrees; with a campfire, take a shovel to the campfire under the cauldron and put it out, and light it again next time with flint and steel. When the cauldron has come down to 40 to 79 degrees, scoop the brew out bottle by bottle with empty glass bottles. Scoop it scalding, or after it has gone stone cold, and the brew still comes out, but its quality drops a notch.

The soup comes in four grades. Stale herbs, a neglected fire or scooping too soon give you Poor: drink it and you draw in qi three tenths faster while breathing, for 60 seconds, and then your lungs are weak for 30 seconds. Middling work brings Common: half again as fast, lasting 90 seconds, with weak lungs for 40 seconds. Handle the heat and the timing well and you get Fine: three quarters faster for a full 120 seconds, with weak lungs for 50 seconds. Only when every step is complete and the nautilus shell went in do you get Superior: you draw in qi twice as fast, the draught lasts 180 seconds, and then your lungs are weak for 60 seconds. To taste the twice-as-fast Superior soup, you still need your own two hands. And if you are careless, let the fire slip and use stale herbs, all you will scoop out in the end is a lump of black Brew Residue, good for nothing.

Remember these steps well and go try your hand at the stove. Do not waste these fine things fished out of the sea.
lore.meridian_brewing.bitter_yellow:
Come, sit here and warm yourself by the fire. This old woman has brewed in this muddy swamp all her life, and these hands are stained so yellow by the herbs that they never wash clean. The brew I teach you today is called Bitter Yellow Paste. Never mind the ugly name, or that it looks like a puddle of mud. Years ago in the old forest a venomous creature bit through my flesh and my leg bone snapped, and it was this one bitter draught that dragged me back from death's door. You can swallow it, or mix it with gunpowder and throw it to save a companion in a pinch. It is so bitter your stomach turns over, and it leaves your limbs soft and weak, but the strength it gives to knit flesh truly saves lives.

To brew this paste, first lay your groundwork. Find the recipe that says Bitter Yellow Paste, hold it in your hand and read it carefully through; then read the brewing scroll and learn the brewing technique, and only then do your hands know the real thing. Such things now and then turn up in the chests of witch huts newly risen in the swamp, or drop from witches of the True Qi realm. Once you have read the recipe, the paper is still yours; you will not lose it.

A beginner sets a Copper Cauldron on a campfire. But a campfire is sun fire that always clings close to 100 degrees and cannot be turned down, far too fierce: Bitter Yellow Paste needs a lower heat than that, and brewed over a campfire it scorches once every 3 seconds, so nothing good comes of it. To brew it well, forge 1 Copper Cauldron and 3 iron ingots into a Witch Cauldron and set it on an Iron Stove. The Iron Stove is cold when first placed and burns sun fire; if it is ever switched to soul fire, press a handful of sand against the cauldron to turn it back. Bring a piece of coal or charcoal to the cauldron and the fire rises one level; give it a stroke of the shovel and it drops one level. Its 4 levels are 75 degrees, 85 degrees, 93 degrees and 100 degrees. Each piece of coal stores 60 seconds of fuel; while the fuel lasts the fire stays put at its level, and only after it has burned out does it sink one level every 60 seconds by itself. For Bitter Yellow Paste, level 2 on the Iron Stove is exactly 85 degrees, the steadiest choice. If you want the finest Superior paste, you must work it with your own hands.

Now the main herb, Dried Moss. Dig some moss blocks from the boggy hollows and lay them out neatly in a Drying Tray. This depends on the sky: it must be daytime, with no rain, and open sky overhead. Let them dry a full 1200 seconds, and only then is the virtue of the moss complete. Raw moss will not go into the pot; it must be dried first. Prepared Dried Moss is strongest within 3 days and weaker each day after; past 9 days only six parts in ten of its virtue remain.

Brewing is fine work, and not a single step may go wrong. Water first: a water bucket poured gives 3 portions, a water bottle gives 1. A Copper Cauldron holds 3 portions and yields 2 bottles; a Witch Cauldron holds 2 and yields 1. With the water in, drop in the Dried Moss first, and the foundation of the brew is set. Then add the base, glowstone dust; if you want a splash brew to throw and save someone, add one gunpowder as well. Once the base is in, do not rush to start. First let the cauldron hold steady between 40 and 79 degrees and soak for a full 10 seconds, so the virtue melts into the water. This is called the warm soak, and it lifts the quality a notch. Keep the Iron Stove at level 1 first, for 75 degrees is just right for soaking; once the soak is done, add coal to bring it up to level 2.

When the soak is done, grip the stick firmly in your right hand, fix your eyes on the heart of the cauldron, summon your qi and cast the brewing technique; that begins the brew. For a full 30 seconds your feet must not stray more than 3 blocks from the heart of the cauldron, and your eyes must not wander or look elsewhere, only at the cauldron or the fire beneath it. It costs a good deal of qi: 6 for a Copper Cauldron, 7.8 for a Witch Cauldron, drawn evenly over the 30 seconds. It takes first from heaven and earth, and if that falls short, from your own meridians; if the two together are not enough for one pot, the brewing technique will not even begin. If both run dry midway, or your mind wanders or you walk off, the brew breaks. Luckily a broken brew is not a total loss: the herbs and the soaking stay in the cauldron, though the qi drawn is not returned and the timing must be counted from the start again. The honey bottle and cobweb already in cannot be added a second time. Catch your breath and you can begin again.

During those 30 seconds your hands must keep to the clock. After the brew starts, between the 6th and 10th second, drop in a honey bottle with your left hand, and the cauldron gives you back an empty glass bottle. Then between the 18th and 22nd second, drop in the catalyst, a cobweb, with your left hand. Early or late within 4 seconds will still do, with weaker virtue; any further off and it is as if you never added it. If you forget the cobweb, however fine your craft, you will never brew a Superior paste in your life.

Keep your eyes on the heat as you brew. Bitter Yellow Paste wants 82 to 90 degrees, and level 2 on the Iron Stove, 85 degrees, sits right inside that. If the fire climbs more than 8 degrees above 90, the pot scorches once every 3 seconds; and anything above 90 degrees boils off a portion of water for nothing every 20 seconds. When the water is gone the whole pot scorches, and a scorched pot wastes all your craft. If you truly must brew on a campfire, pour in a bottle of cold water while the cauldron is not full to press it down: one portion cools a Copper Cauldron by 15 degrees and a Witch Cauldron by 10. But the campfire never rests, so it only helps for a while.

Once the 30 seconds are done and the cauldron settles, do not scoop yet. The fire will not rest by itself: rake it once through the cauldron with a shovel to bring the Iron Stove down to level 1, 75 degrees; a campfire you put out with a shovel. Scoop it too hot and the paste loses a notch of quality, and the same if you wait until it is stone cold. Be patient until the cauldron cools to 40 to 79 degrees, then hold an empty glass bottle to it and scoop slowly, bottle by bottle. Only with fresh herbs, a thorough soak, heat held between 82 and 90 degrees the whole way, herbs added right on time and scooping only after it cools will the pot come out Superior. Be sloppy and let the heat run wild, and you may get Common or even Poor; ruin it so badly that even Poor cannot be kept, and all you scoop is a puddle of black Brew Residue.

Drunk, the grades differ greatly in strength. Poor lasts 16 seconds and restores 12.8 health in all; you move a fifth slower, keep only eighty-five parts in a hundred of your strength, and feel queasy for 10 seconds after. Common lasts 20 seconds and restores 24 health; you move fifteen parts in a hundred slower, keep eighty-five parts in a hundred of your strength, and feel queasy for 8 seconds. Fine lasts 24 seconds and restores 38.4 health; you move fifteen parts in a hundred slower, keep nine tenths of your strength, and feel queasy for 7 seconds. Brewed to Superior, it lasts a full 30 seconds and restores 60 health in all; you move only a tenth slower, keep nine tenths of your strength, and the queasiness lasts just 6 seconds.

Mixed with gunpowder into a splash brew and thrown on a companion, Poor restores 4 health over 10 seconds; Common, 7.2 health over 12 seconds; Fine, 11.2 health over 14 seconds; Superior, 16 health over 16 seconds. But the thrown mist stings the nose, and whoever it lands on is slowed even more: a quarter to two fifths slower, left with only three fifths to three quarters of their quickness.

One last word from this old woman. A Copper Cauldron left in the open under sun and rain rusts easily, and then it carries heat slowly; remember to rub a honeycomb on it to keep the rust off, and scrape it clean with an axe if it rusts. Brewing cannot be rushed. Anxious hearts and shaking hands brew only poison and residue; with a calm heart and clear eyes, this Bitter Yellow Paste can truly save a life. Go on, gather your herbs and try it yourself.
lore.meridian_brewing.insect_lure:
Come, rest your feet under this old woman's thatch. The mist lies heavy in these wetlands, and under every blade of grass there is some creature with too many legs. Today I will teach you Insect Lure Brew. In the old days, when reckless enemies crept into the swamp seeking revenge, this old woman would flick her wrist and throw a bottle at them, and the venomous spiders of the woods and the silverfish of the rock cracks would go mad as if bewitched and fling themselves at him. This brew is far too harsh to drink; it was born to be thrown, so you must add gunpowder and make it a splash brew. When you use it, aim it at someone else, and never splash it at your own feet, or every crawling thing will come for you, and this old woman will not get there in time to bury you.

To brew it, take the recipe that says Insect Lure Brew and read it through several times until you know it by heart; the paper does not wear out. You must also read the brewing scroll thoroughly until the brewing technique is second nature. These life-saving recipes mostly drop from the witches of the True Qi realm deep in the swamp, or are hidden in the chests of newly risen witch huts; they do not come easily.

This brew needs sun fire. Hammer 7 copper ingots into a Copper Cauldron and set it on a campfire. That is sun fire too, but the campfire always clings close to 100 degrees, a good step hotter than this brew wants: too dry, too fierce, you cannot turn it down, and cold water only presses it down for a while. For steadier heat, forge 1 Copper Cauldron and 3 iron ingots into a Witch Cauldron and set it on an Iron Stove. The Iron Stove is cold when first set down and burns sun fire; if one day soul sand or soul soil turns it to soul fire, press a handful of sand against the cauldron and it turns back to sun fire. The stove has four levels of fire: bring charcoal or coal to the cauldron to raise it one level, stroke it with a shovel to lower it one level. Insect Lure Brew wants 84 to 92 degrees. Just add coal up to level 2: exactly 85 degrees, wavering by only 1 degree, just right. Each piece of coal stores 60 seconds of fuel; while it lasts the fire stays put at level 2, and only after it has burned out does it fall one level every 60 seconds. A pot takes only 30 seconds, so just make sure there is enough fuel before you begin. Never add coal while it sits at level 2: one more piece and it jumps to level 3, 93 degrees, out of range. If you must add more, wait until it falls back to level 1.

The ingredients have their rules too. The main herb is Berry Mash: press sweet berries onto a grindstone and a portion is ground out at once. Prepared herbs are fullest in virtue if they go into the pot within 3 days; left longer they fade day by day, and from the 9th day only six parts in ten remain. If you take a shortcut and throw raw sweet berries in, they will not go in; they must be mashed first. The accessory is a pinch of sugar. The catalyst is a honeycomb; in this brew the honeycomb leads the medicine, and holding it will not wax the cauldron, so grip it without worry. For the base, have glowstone dust ready, plus one gunpowder, which matters most of all.

When you are ready, water first. One water bucket gives 3 portions; with water bottles you add 1 portion at a time. A Copper Cauldron holds 3 portions and yields 2 bottles; a Witch Cauldron holds 2 and yields 1. With the water in, drop in the Berry Mash first; once the main herb lands, the foundation is set. Then drop in the glowstone dust and the gunpowder as the base. Do not rush to start the brew. Keep the cauldron steady between 40 and 79 degrees and let it soak quietly in the warm water for a full 10 seconds; the stove left at level 1, 75 degrees, is just right. Only after a full soak does the sweet-sour strength of the berries melt free.

When the soak is done, hold the stick steady in your right hand, fix your eyes on the heart of the cauldron and cast the brewing technique; that begins the brew. A pot takes a full 30 seconds. Your feet must not stray more than 3 blocks from the heart of the cauldron, and your eyes must not leave the cauldron and the fire beneath it even for a blink. A Copper Cauldron draws 6 qi for this pot and a Witch Cauldron 7.8, taken evenly over the 30 seconds. It draws first from the qi of heaven and earth around you; when that falls short, it takes from the cultivation in your meridians. If the two together do not make up one pot, the brewing technique will not even begin; if both run dry halfway, the technique breaks on the spot. But even when a pot breaks midway, the herbs and the soaking stay at the bottom of the cauldron. Only the qi already drawn is not returned, the timing must be counted from the start again, and the sugar and honeycomb already in cannot be added a second time. Just begin the brew anew.

For these 30 seconds the timing rests entirely on your silent count. Between the 6th and 10th second after the brew begins, drop the sugar into the cauldron with your left hand. Then between the 18th and 22nd second, drop the honeycomb in steadily with your left hand. Those seconds are the best fit; early or late within 4 seconds, some virtue remains, but any further off and it is no better than throwing it away.

Through that half minute the heat must stay pressed between 84 and 92 degrees. Once it leaves that range, the virtue will not brew in fully. Insect Lure Brew will not scorch if the fire runs high, but above 90 degrees a portion of water boils off for nothing every 20 seconds; when the water runs low and boils dry, the pot scorches through and not even the immortals can save it.

When the 30 seconds are up and the cauldron goes quiet, do not be impatient to scoop. The fire below will not back off by itself: rake it once through the cauldron with a shovel to bring the Iron Stove down to level 1, 75 degrees; a campfire you put out with a shovel. When the cauldron cools to between 40 and 79 degrees, scoop bottle after bottle with empty glass bottles; scoop it scalding or stone cold and the quality drops a notch. Fresh herbs, a full 10-second soak in warm water, heat held in range from start to finish, accessory and catalyst added on time, scooping after it cools: only with every one of these, and the honeycomb leading the way, will you scoop out a Superior Insect Lure Brew. Without the honeycomb, however heaven-reaching your skill, Fine is the most you will get. Let the fire slip or miss the timing and you get Common or even Poor; be careless beyond that and all you scoop may be a puddle of black Brew Residue.

Brews of different grades differ greatly in force. A Poor brew thrown splashes 3 blocks wide, its scent lasts only 15 seconds and draws the many-legged venomous creatures within 12 blocks, but not even half a silverfish crawls out of the ground. A Common brew splashes 3 blocks, its scent lingers 20 seconds and stirs the creatures within 16 blocks, and 1 silverfish burrows out where it lands to help bite. A Fine brew splashes 3.5 blocks, its scent lingers 25 seconds and draws the creatures within 20 blocks, and 2 silverfish crawl out of the cracks. Brew it Superior with true mastery and a single throw splashes 4 blocks around; the thick scent spreads for a full 30 seconds, every spider and crawling thing within 24 blocks smells it and charges in a frenzy, and 3 silverfish break out of the earth right there to chew your enemy to the bone.

If you want the Superior drop that calls up 3 silverfish, in the end it comes from the stick in your own hand, patiently tending the fire. This old woman has told you all she knows. Go fetch your sweet berries, and be quick about it.
lore.meridian_brewing.depletion:
Come, sit closer and shut the vent. The damp is heavy out in the swamp; it gets into your bones. The brew this old one teaches today is Depletion Brew. It is not for saving or nursing anyone: it is a vicious recipe you throw when enemies or fierce creatures come at you, to cripple their limbs and eat at their sinews and bones. Long ago in this mud I ran into a witch of the True Qi realm who had fled down from the north. We fought until my bones nearly fell apart, and when I finally put her down I found this recipe on her, along with a brewing scroll. Learn the brewing technique in that scroll thoroughly, and read the paper in your hand carefully, or you could throw heavenly treasures into the pot and still nothing would stir. Keep the recipe tucked in your coat; reading it will not destroy it.

Depletion Brew is cruel: it cannot be drunk, only made into a splash brew to throw. If one day you forget the gunpowder, the brewing technique will not even begin.

First, the furnace and the fire. This brew is deeply yin and must be burned on soul fire. If you are short of means, hammer 7 copper ingots into a Copper Cauldron and set it on a soul campfire. A Copper Cauldron on a soul campfire always clings close to 100 degrees, locked there and impossible to adjust, but luckily this brew wants a roaring fire and fits it just right. Only, if the top of the Copper Cauldron is open to the sky and the rain, over time it rusts and carries heat more slowly; rub a honeycomb on it to keep the rust off, and scrape it with an axe once it has rusted.

My advice: once your craft is practised, switch to a Witch Cauldron on an Iron Stove. Forge 1 Copper Cauldron and 3 iron ingots into a Witch Cauldron and set it on an Iron Stove. A newly placed Iron Stove is cold and burns sun fire; take soul sand or soul soil and press it against the cauldron, and it turns to soul fire. The stove has four levels: add a piece of coal or charcoal to raise one level, tap the cauldron with a shovel to lower one. Each piece of coal stores 60 seconds of fuel; while it lasts the fire stays put at its level, and only after it has burned out does it sink one level every 60 seconds by itself, so just make sure there is enough fuel before you begin.

The main herb for this brew is Withered Bush Ash. Go cut some ordinary grass, build a campfire, and roast the grass on it for 30 seconds until it is a scorched handful of ash, then gather it up. Raw grass will not go into the cauldron; it must be roasted to ash first. This prepared ash is delicate: within 3 days of coming off the fire it is strongest, and the longer it sits the more it fades; past the 9th day only six parts in ten of its power remain. So when you brew, roast it fresh and use it right away.

Fill the water first. Pour a water bucket into the cauldron for 3 portions, or a water bottle for 1. A full Copper Cauldron holds 3 portions, a Witch Cauldron 2. Once the water is in, drop in the Withered Bush Ash first; once the main herb lands, what you are brewing is settled. Next comes the base: a glowstone dust, and right after it, be sure to add a gunpowder!

Once those are in, do not rush to bring it to the boil; soak first. Hold the cauldron between 40 and 79 degrees and let the ash and the base soak in warm water for a full 10 seconds; once the herbs are steeped through, the foundation runs deep. With an Iron Stove, leave it at level 1 first, for 75 degrees is just right for soaking; once the soak is done, add coal to raise the level.

When the soak is done, raise the fire. Depletion Brew is the hottest of the six recipes: its heat must bite between 92 and 100 degrees. Level 3 on a Iron Stove is exactly 93 degrees, wavering by only 1, steady as a mountain; a soul campfire clings close to 100 degrees, right inside the range, and will do too. This brew will not scorch however fierce the fire, so never pour cold water in: one bottle cools a Copper Cauldron by 15 degrees and a Witch Cauldron by 10, and one splash knocks it out of range. Still, above 90 degrees a portion of water boils off every 20 seconds; when the water runs low and boils dry, the pot scorches through all the same!

When the heat is about right, hold the stick in your right hand, face the cauldron squarely, settle your mind and cast the brewing technique. The brew lasts a full 30 seconds. Have plenty of qi stored in your body: a Copper Cauldron takes 6 qi per pot and a Witch Cauldron 7.8, drawn slowly over the 30 seconds. If the qi of heaven and earth around you is enough, it takes from there first; if not, it pulls hard from the meridians you have opened. If the two together are not enough for one pot, the technique will not even begin; if both run dry halfway, the technique scatters and the pot breaks on the spot. While brewing, you must not move more than 3 blocks from the heart of the cauldron, and your eyes must not leave the cauldron or the fire below for an instant; turn your head to look at something else, or walk off, and the pot breaks. Do not panic if it breaks: the herbs and the soaking are still in there. Only the qi already drawn is not returned, the timing must be counted from the start again, and the spider eye and the rose already in cannot be added a second time. Steady your mind and you can begin anew.

Your left hand must not be idle in those 30 seconds. Count the beats after the brew begins; between the 6th and 10th second, drop a fermented spider eye into the cauldron as the accessory. Early or late, the strength suffers; more than 4 seconds off and it is almost as if you never added it. Once the accessory is in, keep watching the fire, and between the 20th and 24th second, drop in that baleful wither rose as the catalyst. Only with this catalyst can you reach Superior; without it, however heaven-reaching your skill, Fine is the most you will get.

When the full 30 seconds are done, the glow in the cauldron fades and the brew is finished. But the fire below does not go out with it, so above all do not rush to scoop with an empty glass bottle! Boiling brew scooped out loses a notch of quality, and so does brew left until stone cold. With an Iron Stove, rake it a few times through the cauldron with a shovel to bring it down to level 1, 75 degrees; with a soul campfire, put it out with a stroke of the shovel. When the cauldron cools to between 40 and 79 degrees, scoop it out bottle by bottle with empty glass bottles. A Copper Cauldron gives 2 bottles, a Witch Cauldron 1.

With rough craft, a wandering fire and badly timed herbs, you scoop out a Poor brew. Thrown on the ground it splashes only 3 blocks, strikes 1 to 2 places on a body and lasts 10 seconds, leaving nineteen parts in twenty of their stamina and nine tenths of their speed, and it eats away 5 points of flesh as well. A somewhat better Common brew splashes 3.5 blocks, strikes 2 places and lasts 13 seconds, leaving ninety-two parts in a hundred of their stamina and seventeen parts in twenty of their speed, and eats away 5 points of flesh. A carefully brewed Fine one splashes 4 blocks, strikes 2 to 3 places and lasts a full 16 seconds, leaving eighty-eight parts in a hundred of their stamina and four fifths of their speed, and eats away 6 points of flesh. And if every step of yours was exact and the catalyst went in, the Superior brew you gather splashes 4.5 blocks when thrown and bites hard into 3 vital places; for a full 20 seconds it leaves only eighty-four parts in a hundred of their stamina, slows them to three quarters of their speed, and eats away 7 points of flesh on the spot!

Remember: do not rush, watch the fire closely, and keep a steady hand with the herbs. Go light the campfire out back, and roast your grass first.
lore.meridian_brewing.armor_rot:
Come, sit by Granny. The damp in this bog is heavy; pull that old stump over to rest your feet on. See this big cauldron churning over the faint blue-green fire? Today Granny will teach you a vicious, overbearing brew called Armor Rot Brew. In years past, enemies wrapped in iron shells and armored corpses from the deep mountains threw sparks when a blade struck them, and ordinary means could not touch them. Then it all came down to a splash of Armor Rot Brew: wherever it lands on armor, the iron or copper there rots away as if gnawed by demons, and even the thickest plate goes several parts softer. Only one thing: it cannot eat golden armor at all, and netherite armor it eats only half as much. This brew must never be drunk; it was born to be thrown at enemies, so you must add gunpowder to the pot, or the brew will not start at all.

To brew it, you must first master two things. Study the paper bearing the Armor Rot Brew recipe carefully until you see through it; the paper will not spoil. And you must read the brewing scroll thoroughly and practise the brewing technique in your heart. Both treasures depend on luck: you will have to deal with witches of the True Qi realm, or creep into the witch huts newly risen in the swamp and rummage through their chests.

The vessels cannot be careless either. A beginner hammers 7 copper ingots into a Copper Cauldron, which holds 3 portions of water and yields 2 bottles. If its top is open to sun, moon, wind and rain, it slowly rusts and carries heat sluggishly; rub a honeycomb on it to keep the rust off, and scrape away deep rust with an axe. When you have finished your apprenticeship, forge 1 Copper Cauldron and 3 iron ingots into a Witch Cauldron, which holds 2 portions, yields 1 bottle and lets the heat through faster. The Copper Cauldron sits on a soul campfire, a faint yin flame. Its heat always clings close to 100 degrees and cannot be adjusted. Granny advises you to use a Witch Cauldron on an Iron Stove. A freshly placed Iron Stove is cold and burns sun fire; press a handful of soul sand or soul soil against the cauldron and the fire turns to soul fire. The stove has 4 levels: 75 degrees, 85 degrees, 93 degrees and 100 degrees. Touch coal or charcoal to the cauldron and the fire rises a level; tap it with a shovel and it drops a level. Each piece of coal stores 60 seconds of fuel; while it lasts the fire stays put at its level, and only after it has burned out does it sink one level every 60 seconds. Armor Rot Brew wants 90 to 98 degrees; raise the stove to level 3, exactly 93 degrees, the steadiest of all.

Preparing the herbs tests your craft the most. The main herb is Poison Potato Slices. First make a Herb Knife, an iron ingot on top and a stick below. Hold the Herb Knife in your right hand and a poisonous potato in your left, and press down to slice it slowly, one cut at a time; each cut takes 1 second, and if you let go midway that cut does not count. Herbs cut and in the pot within 3 days are at their fullest and fiercest; delay and they slacken day by day, and past 9 days only six parts in ten of their strength remain. A raw poisonous potato will not go into the cauldron; it must be cut into slices. The accessory is redstone dust, and the catalyst is dragon's breath. Without the catalyst, however good your craft, you will never brew the top Superior grade.

When brewing, follow the method step by step. Water first: a water bucket poured gives 3 portions, a water bottle gives 1. Once it is full, drop in the Poison Potato Slices, and the name of the brew is settled. Next the base: sprinkle in a handful of glowstone dust and throw in a gunpowder. Do not rush to start yet; let the cauldron soak slowly between 40 and 79 degrees for a full 10 seconds, and only then is the foundation solid. Then grip the stick in your right hand, fix your eyes on the heart of the cauldron and cast the brewing technique, brewing a full 30 seconds. A Copper Cauldron takes 6 qi per pot and a Witch Cauldron 7.8, spread evenly over the 30 seconds. It takes first from the spirit qi of heaven and earth around you, and then from the meridians you have opened; if the two together are not enough for one pot, the technique will not even begin, and if both give out halfway, the pot stops at once. During those 30 seconds your eyes must stay fixed on the cauldron or the fire below, and your body must not go more than 3 blocks from the heart of the cauldron. Let your mind wander or walk off and the breath of the brew breaks. But do not panic: the herbs and the soaking remain in the broken pot. Only the qi already drawn is not returned, the timing must be counted from the start again, and the redstone dust and dragon's breath already in cannot be added a second time. Just begin anew.

Once brewing starts, time is precious. Between the 6th and 10th second, drop in the redstone dust with your left hand; between the 20th and 24th second, send the dragon's breath into the cauldron, and the cauldron, taking the dragon's breath, gives you back an empty glass bottle. Early or late within 4 seconds, the strength will just about do; any further off and the herb is simply thrown away. Watch the fire closely: this brew will not scorch if the fire runs high, but once the heat leaves 90 to 98 degrees its virtue will not brew in fully. Above 90 degrees 1 portion of water steams off every 20 seconds; when the water runs low, do not let it boil dry and scorch the pot. If you brew on that soul campfire, the heat clings close to 100 degrees, a little above the range, and a bottle of cold water only holds it for a while: a Copper Cauldron cools 15 degrees per bottle, a Witch Cauldron 10.

When the 30 seconds are done and the scent of the brew drifts out, do not rush to scoop with a bottle. The fire below will not rest by itself: rake it a few times through the cauldron with a shovel to bring the Iron Stove down to level 1, 75 degrees; put a soul campfire out with the shovel. Fresh off the fire it is scalding; scoop it scalding or stone cold and the quality drops a notch. Wait patiently for the cauldron to cool to 40 to 79 degrees, then scoop it up bottle by bottle with empty glass bottles.

Fresh herbs, a full soak, heat held between 90 and 98 degrees, accessory and catalyst in on time, and collecting the brew after it cools: only a brew made this way is called Superior. Without the dragon's breath, however masterful your brewing, Fine is the most it can be. Cut corners and let the heat run wild, and you get Common or even Poor; with stale herbs and the fire all wrong, all you scoop is a lump of black Brew Residue.

Once brewed, its force when thrown varies greatly. A Poor Armor Rot Brew splashes only 3 blocks on the ground, hits 1 to 2 pieces of an enemy's armor and lasts 10 seconds; every second the piece rots away by one part in two hundred, and its hardness there falls to eighty-five parts in a hundred. A Common one splashes 3 blocks, hits 2 pieces and works for 12 seconds, rotting three parts in four hundred each second and leaving the armor four fifths as strong. A Fine one throws 3.5 blocks, covers 2 to 3 pieces and torments them for 15 seconds, rotting one part in a hundred each second and leaving the armor seven tenths as strong. And a clear Superior Armor Rot Brew lands in a 4-block wave, bites hard into 3 pieces of armor and rots them for a full 20 seconds, three parts in two hundred each second, leaving the hard plate there only three fifths as firm on the spot. Iron bones and copper body or not, he will be at your mercy.

That is the old way, all of it. Grip your stick firmly and go, and mind you do not burn your hands.
lore.meridian_brewing.charm:
Come, sit by this old one's hearth, and warm your hands before you listen. Today I will pass on the recipe that tests your patience more than any other: Charm Brew. Long ago, deep in the black swamp, I ran into a great thick-skinned wild boar, and it was a bottle of this that saved my old life. Thrown, its mist rises off whatever living thing it lands on, and however fierce its nature, it first freezes stiff on the spot for a moment; then its eyes go hazy, and it reels about bewitched for a while, letting you lead it as you please. But remember this: once it comes back to its senses, it stays on guard for at least 10 seconds, and another throw will not work in that time.

To brew it, first calm your heart and read the paper bearing the recipe over and over until you understand it fully, then go and understand the brewing scroll and learn the brewing technique; only then have you stepped through the door. If you cannot find these in the chests of witch huts newly risen in the swamp, you will have to get them from the witches who have reached True Qi. This brew is fiery by nature and can only be made into a splash brew to throw; drinking it will never do. Before you start brewing, you must add a gunpowder; forget this one and the brewing technique will not even begin.

The soul fire from a soul campfire clings to 100 degrees and cannot be brought down at all. This is the most delicate of the six recipes and wants the gentlest heat: it must settle steadily between 80 and 88 degrees, and more than 8 degrees above that it scorches. On a campfire it scorches once every 3 seconds. Even if you press it down with cold water, one bottle cooling a Copper Cauldron by 15 degrees and a Witch Cauldron by 10, it only holds for a while, and nine times out of ten what you scoop out is a puddle of residue. Set an Iron Stove at the bottom, and on top a Witch Cauldron forged from 1 Copper Cauldron and 3 iron ingots. The Witch Cauldron carries heat quickly.

This Iron Stove is cold when first set down and burns sun fire; press a handful of soul sand or soul soil against the cauldron, and once the nature of the fire turns, it becomes the soul fire we need. The stove has four levels: touch coal or charcoal to the cauldron to raise one level, stroke it with a shovel to lower one. Set it at level 2: exactly 85 degrees, wavering by only 1 degree, settled right inside the range. Each piece of coal stores 60 seconds of fuel; while it lasts the fire stays put at level 2, and only after it has burned out does it drop one level every 60 seconds by itself. When it drops to level 1, add another piece and it is back at level 2. Never add coal while it is at level 2: one more and it jumps to 93 degrees, out of range.

With the fire ready, the herbs cannot be careless. The main herb is Dried Poppy. On a bright clear day, with nothing at all overhead, lay freshly picked poppies in a Drying Tray to take in the dry air of the day, and let them dry a full 1200 seconds. Raw poppies cannot go into the cauldron; they must be dried first. The dried flowers are strongest within 3 days; the longer they sit the more their virtue fades, and past the 9th day only six parts in ten remain, and nothing good will come of them.

When brewing, the order must never be muddled. First fill the Witch Cauldron with a water bucket, which fills its two portions. Next drop in the Dried Poppy; with that, the cauldron knows which recipe it is brewing. Then quickly add a glowstone dust as the base, and a gunpowder to set it on the splash path. Do not push the fire up yet: leave the Iron Stove at level 1, 75 degrees, and let the warm water sit between 40 and 79 degrees, soaking quietly for a full 10 seconds; once the soak is done, add coal to bring it up to level 2. If this step is steeped through, the virtue can fully come out.

When the soak is done, take a deep breath and begin! Grip the stick in your right hand, fix your eyes on the cauldron or the flames beneath it, and cast the brewing technique. The brew lasts 30 seconds; your body must not move more than 3 blocks from the heart of the cauldron, and your gaze must not drift elsewhere. A Witch Cauldron takes 7.8 qi from you evenly over the pot; a Copper Cauldron of 7 copper ingots takes 6. If the spirit qi of heaven and earth is not enough, the rest is drawn from the meridians you have opened; if the two together are not enough for one pot, the technique will not even begin, and if both run dry halfway, or you step too far away, the pot breaks on the spot. The herbs and the soaking stay in the cauldron, but the qi drawn is not returned, the timing must be counted from the start again, and the berry and the shard already in cannot be added a second time. You have to begin anew, all that trouble for nothing.

Once brewing begins, count the moments silently. Between the 8th and 12th second, quickly drop in a glow berry with your left hand; early or late, its strength suffers. Keep counting, and between the 22nd and 26th second, throw in the catalyst, an amethyst shard. Remember well: without this amethyst shard, however good your craft, you will never in your life brew a Superior Charm Brew.

For these 30 seconds the heat must hold between 80 and 88 degrees. If the fire climbs more than 8 degrees above 88, the brew scorches once every 3 seconds; and if it goes past 90 degrees, a portion of water is steamed away every 20 seconds. Once the water boils dry, the whole pot burns to charcoal.

When the 30 seconds have passed and the brew settles, above all do not rush to scoop with an empty glass bottle! Scalding brew scooped out loses a notch of quality, and so does brew left until stone cold. The fire below will not rest by itself: rake it once through the cauldron with a shovel to bring the Iron Stove down to level 1, 75 degrees. Be patient until the water in the cauldron cools to between 40 and 79 degrees, then scoop it out one bottle at a time. A Witch Cauldron gives exactly 1 bottle.

The quality of the pot depends entirely on the care your hands just took: fresh herbs, a full soak, a precise fire, unhurried collecting, and the brews come out differently. The roughest Poor brew splashes only 2.5 blocks and freezes a creature for 0.8 seconds, and the daze lasts just 3 seconds before it comes to. A Common one, with the fire kept more orderly, splashes 3 blocks, freezes for 1.0 second and bewitches for 4 seconds. A better Fine brew also splashes 3 blocks but freezes stiff for 1.3 seconds and dazes for a full 5 seconds. Only a Superior brew, with the catalyst in and every step done well, spreads its mist 3.5 blocks at once, freezes whatever it hits for a full 1.6 seconds and bewitches it for 6 seconds. In a dangerous place, that extra moment is enough to escape over several mountains.

If any step goes astray, if the brew scorches a few times or you did not tend it well, what you scoop out at the end is a lump of black Brew Residue, good for nothing. This old one has boiled her hair white in this swamp over these few steps of fire and herbs. Take your herbs now, and go try it at the furnace.
lore.meridian_brewing.fire_elixir:
Come, sit by the campfire and warm your hands, and listen to this old granny ramble a bit. The damp runs heavy in our swamp, but the brew I am teaching you today is the fiercest, driest thing under the heavens, called Blazing Salve Elixir. It is the one among the Five Elements elixirs that runs strictly through Fire. Sealed in a clear glass bottle, it can only be tilted back and swallowed down your gullet—it must never, ever be splashed, and the cauldron will not stomach a single speck of gunpowder either. In years past, some young folks practicing fire spells found drawing in the spiritual qi of heaven and earth far too slow, so right before making a move, they would take a small sip. That fiery energy rolled straight down their throats into their bellies on the spot, saving them the bitter work of half a day of breathing exercises.

If you want to brew this, you have got to open your eyes to the wider world first. Go find yourself a parchment with this recipe written down, hold it in your hands and study it thoroughly, then read a brewing scroll to learn the hand-form brewing art. These things have to be begged off witches who have cultivated to the True Qi realm, or found if you strike it lucky rummaging through chests in freshly built witch huts deep in the swamp.

First, let us talk fire and furnace. Brewing this medicine demands blazing Yang fire. The crudest way is hammering 7 copper ingots into a copper cauldron and propping it atop a campfire. A campfire gives Yang fire, but the temperature always wobbles around 100 degrees; you cannot adjust the flame, and it is too aggressive. Granny advises you to take a copper cauldron, add 3 iron ingots to forge it into a witch cauldron and set an iron stove underneath. A newly placed iron brazier is cold, but it counts as Yang fire, and if it goes out, filling it with sand also makes it Yang fire. Tap the cauldron with coal or charcoal once, and the heat goes up by 1 tier while storing up 60 seconds of fuel; if you think the fire is too high, tap the cauldron with an iron shovel to drop it down 1 tier.

Next is preparing your ingredients. Ordinary herbs, woods, and minerals all need processing first, and properly processed ingredients have their fullest potency within 3 days; after 9 days, only 60 percent of their medicinal strength remains. The main ingredient for this Blazing Salve Elixir just happens to be an exception, though: it uses Blaze Powder crushed from blaze rods, a naturally scorching thing that needs no processing and can go right into the cauldron. For the secondary ingredient, you must prepare a piece of Magma Cream, and for the guide medicine, a Fire Charge.

When you start brewing, pour water into the cauldron first. Emptying a water bucket once gives 3 portions of water, and emptying a water bottle once gives 1 portion. A copper cauldron can hold 3 portions of water to yield 2 bottles, and a witch cauldron can hold 2 portions of water to yield 1 bottle. Once it is filled with water, cast the Blaze Powder into the cauldron, and the destiny of this batch is settled. Next, toss in the base ingredient, Glowstone Dust. Mind you, do not get any crooked ideas about tossing gunpowder in; even if you throw it in, the cauldron will not accept it. Once the ingredients are in, do not rush to start brewing. Let the cauldron temperature warm gently between 40 and 79 degrees, soaking for a full 10 seconds. This step is called soaking—only when the water thoroughly seeps into the powder can its medicinal nature unfold later on.

Once it has soaked long enough, it is time to start the brewing. This step drains your vitality fiercely: a copper cauldron drains 6 yuan of true qi from you, and a witch cauldron drains 7.8 yuan, steadily drawn out across the 30 seconds of brewing. It draws true qi from heaven and earth first; if there is not enough, it forcefully siphons from the opened meridians in your body. If the true qi in your whole body cannot meet this tally, the cauldron will not make a single peep. Hold a wooden stick in your right hand, fix your eyes firmly on the cauldron, and begin performing the brewing art. For the entirety of those 30 seconds of brewing, your feet cannot stray more than 3 blocks from the center of the cauldron, and your eyes must be locked onto the cauldron or the flames beneath it. The moment you get distracted and look away, or take too big a step, the medicinal vapor breaks on the spot. If it breaks, it is not completely ruined—the ingredients and the soaking work remain in the pot, so steady your mind and you can start another round.

During those 30 seconds, your hands cannot sit idle. Once the brewing starts, count in your head: between the 8th and 12th second, take the Magma Cream in your left hand and toss it into the cauldron as the secondary ingredient; then keep counting patiently, and between the 22nd and 26th second, toss in the Fire Charge with your left hand as the guide medicine. The timing for these two ingredients hitting the pot is crucial beyond measure. If you are off by within 4 seconds, early or late, the potency takes a hit; if you miss by even more, throwing them in is no different from tossing pebbles. What is more important, if you do not add the guide medicine, you could brew till the sky cracks and never touch the threshold of Superior—at most, you will get Fine.

All the while, your eyes must keep a tight watch on the temperature. The heat zone for Blazing Salve Elixir lies between 88 and 96 degrees. An iron stove set to tier 3 hits exactly 93 degrees, wavering by only 1 degree—steady as an old rock, suiting this elixir's temper perfectly. If the temperature climbs more than 8 degrees higher than the top of the heat zone at 96 degrees, the cauldron scorches once every 3 seconds. As long as the temperature stays above 90 degrees, 1 portion of water will evaporate away every 20 seconds, and once the water boils dry, the whole pot burns to cinders. If you only have a campfire on hand and see the flames leaping toward 100 degrees, press it down with cold water right away: adding 1 portion of cold water lowers a copper cauldron by 15 degrees, and a witch cauldron by 10 degrees. You have got to be nimble with your hands.

Once you have finally lasted through the 30 seconds and the medicinal aroma spills out of the cauldron, do not you dare rush to scoop it up with empty glass bottles. Scalding-hot elixir slurry cannot hold its spiritual qi yet; you have to wait patiently for the cauldron's fire to recede, and only when the cauldron temperature drops between 40 and 79 degrees should you take your empty glass bottles and scoop it out, bottle by bottle. If you are too hasty gathering the medicine, even the finest brew goes to waste.

How well the medicine turns out depends entirely on the skill of your craft. Fresh ingredients, soaked long enough, temperature held steady within the heat zone, secondary and guide ingredients tossed in without the slightest error, scooped out only after cooling down, and never once scorched—brew it like that, and only then do you get exquisite, Superior Blazing Salve Elixir. A slight blemish makes it Fine, a bit worse makes it Common, and anything made in a clumsy fluster turns out Poor. If you scorch it on top of blunders, what you ladle out will be nothing but a black puddle of dregs.

Drink down this draught, and a Poor one grants 0.6 yuan of fire-attribute true qi, a Common one grants 1 yuan, a Fine one grants 1.5 yuan, and a Superior one reaches as high as 2.4 yuan. As that elixir trickles down your throat, the true qi pours on the spot into the fire-attribute meridians you have already opened in your body—whether it is the Heart Meridian or the Small Intestine Meridian, so long as it is an unblocked fire meridian, it will fill right up. But if you have not opened a single meridian belonging to fire, or if they are already packed full to the brim with true qi, then that gulp is drunk in vain, and that precious true qi scatters away without a trace on the spot.

Lastly, this old woman ought to rap you on the head with my cane and hammer in one life-saving rule: when you drink this brew, an elixir toxin called Inner Scorch settles in your gut, taking a full 300 seconds to disperse, and no matter how many buckets of milk you guzzle down, you cannot wash it out. While Inner Scorch clings to you, your stomach empties awful fast. If those 300 seconds have not passed yet and you get greedy and chug down another bottle of Blazing Salve Elixir, the true qi from that bottle is cut straight in half, while the Inner Scorch inside you stacks another layer deeper, forcing you to suffer through 300 seconds all over again from the start. If that elixir toxin stacks up to the third layer, not only will your belly stick to your backbone with hunger, but every 20 seconds it will feel like a red-hot branding iron has dropped right into your chest, searing you hard; at that point, you could drink all the Blazing Salve Elixir in the world and you will not squeeze out half a drop of true qi—you will just be heaping on another 300 seconds of pure misery for nothing. A snake trying to swallow an elephant will only choke on its greed; once you have finished a bottle, sit tight and wait till the fire in your belly burns clean out. You hear me?
lore.meridian_brewing.overview:
Come, sit by this old one's hearth. The swamp is damp and the plants rot sour, yet all the making of heaven and earth is hidden in this muddy pond. When this old one was your age, to learn the ways of brewing I contended in the woods with witches who had reached the True Qi realm, and suffered no end of hardship before I found those brewing scrolls and recipe papers, on them and in the chests of witch huts newly risen in the swamp. Now that you have come to learn from me, you must keep the rules of the craft in your heart one by one, without the least vagueness.

To brew, first get your tools in order. Sticks and planks make a nine-slot Drying Tray, used for drying moss blocks and poppies; remember it must be daytime, with no rain, in a place open to the sky, and only when they have soaked up their fill of daylight are they any use. To slice a poisonous potato you need a Herb Knife, made with an iron ingot on top and a stick beneath. Six iron ingots around a campfire make an Iron Brazier; that brazier is only for making the Iron Stove and goes into no furnace. Then seven iron ingots around the Iron Brazier, with a stone brick set in the top middle, make the Iron Stove, which you will rely on for all your fire tending. As for the cauldron that holds the brew, a beginner hammers 7 copper ingots into a Copper Cauldron, which holds 3 portions of water and gives 2 bottles. But copper is precious: if its top is open to wind and rain, over time it grows green rust, and each stage of rust carries heat more slowly than the last. Scrape the rust off with an axe, or rub on a coat of wax with a honeycomb to keep it off. Later, when your craft is refined, add 3 iron ingots to a Copper Cauldron to forge a Witch Cauldron, which carries heat faster and holds 2 portions of water, 1 bottle a pot.

A campfire gives sun fire and a soul campfire breathes soul fire, but these wood fires are wild: the heat always clings close to 100 degrees and you cannot turn them down. Recipes that want a lower heat do not brew well on a campfire. While the cauldron is not full, a bottle of cold water presses the heat down 15 degrees, but the campfire never rests, and before long it burns back up.

This Iron Stove is a brewer's real treasure: its flame is very steady, trembling within just 1 degree. It has four levels: 75 degrees, 85 degrees, 93 degrees and 100 degrees. Bring coal or charcoal to the cauldron and the fire leaps up a level; give the cauldron a light stroke with a shovel and it drops a level. Each piece of coal stores 60 seconds of fuel; while it lasts the fire stays put at its level, and only after it has burned out does it sink one level every 60 seconds by itself. A freshly placed stove is cold and burns sun fire: press a handful of sand against the cauldron to turn it to sun fire, or a handful of soul sand or soul soil to turn it to soul fire. The Witch Cauldron carries heat quickly, and a bottle of cold water cools it by 10 degrees.

Brewing by hand has strict rules. Read the recipe paper in your hand thoroughly, then understand the brewing scroll and learn the brewing technique. Above all, herbs must be fresh: a raw main herb will not go into the cauldron and must be prepared first. Even prepared properly, it must go into the pot within 3 days to be at its strongest; after that its virtue fades day by day, and past the 9th day only six parts in ten remain.

The order of a pot must not slip half a step. Pour water into the cauldron first: a water bucket gives 3 portions, a water bottle 1. Then add the main herb; once it lands in the cauldron, which brew it is becomes fixed. Then add glowstone dust as the base; for a splash brew to throw, whether to harm or to heal, add a gunpowder too; for Qi Gathering Soup, which can only be drunk, gunpowder will not go in. Once the base is in, hold the cauldron between 40 and 79 degrees and soak a full 10 seconds, so the virtue opens and the foundation grows rich. With an Iron Stove, keep it at level 1 while soaking, for 75 degrees is just right; once the soak is done, add coal to raise the level, and start the brew when the heat has come up.

After the soak, hold the stick steady in your right hand, set your eyes on the heart of the cauldron or the flame below, and cast the brewing technique to begin! A Copper Cauldron takes 6 qi and a Witch Cauldron 7.8, flowing evenly into the cauldron over a full 30 seconds. If there is qi in the heaven and earth around you, it takes that; when it runs short, it draws from the meridians you have opened. If the two together are not enough for one pot, the brewing technique will not even begin. For those 30 seconds your body must stay within 3 blocks of the heart of the cauldron and your eyes must never leave it. The slightest distraction, both sources running dry midway, or the furnace being broken, and the breath of the brew snaps at once. Do not panic if it breaks: the herbs and the virtue soaked into them are still in the cauldron. Only the qi already drawn is not returned, the heat and the timing must be counted from the start again, and the accessory and catalyst already in cannot be added a second time. Even out your breathing and begin anew.

During the 30 seconds, keep to the seconds written on the recipe and drop in the accessory and the catalyst with your left hand right on time. Early or late within 4 seconds, the strength will still do; off by too much, it is as if you never added it; and without the catalyst, however good your craft, you will never get a Superior brew. Watching the fire matters even more: the heat must stay pinned inside the range the recipe wants. More than 8 degrees above that range and the brew scorches a layer every 3 seconds; once the heat passes 90 degrees, a portion of water boils away every 20 seconds, and when the water is gone the whole pot burns at once! When it is done, do not be hasty, for the fire below will not rest by itself: rake an Iron Stove a few times through the cauldron with a shovel to bring it down to level 1, 75 degrees; put a campfire out with the shovel, and light it again next time with flint and steel. When the cauldron has cooled to 40 to 79 degrees, scoop it up bottle by bottle with empty glass bottles. If you scoop it scalding, or only after it has gone stone cold, the brew still comes out, but its quality drops a notch.

Once brewed, the bottle tells the truth. Fresh herbs, a full 10-second soak, a steady fire, accessory and catalyst added exactly on time, and collecting after it cools: only what such care produces is Superior. One step down is Fine; plain and ordinary is Common; with flustered hands and a wild fire you get Poor; if the brew scorched several times and the fire was all wrong, all you scoop out with a bottle is a puddle of pitch-black Brew Residue; and if the water boiled dry and the pot scorched, there is not even residue to scoop.

Six recipes have come down through this old one: Qi Gathering Soup, drunk to aid breathing and gather qi; Bitter Yellow Paste, drunk or thrown to restore health; Insect Lure Brew, which draws venomous creatures; Depletion Brew, which eats at flesh and limbs; Armor Rot Brew, which ruins a foe's armor; and Charm Brew, which bewitches the mind. The ways of brewing are all written in the recipes, one by one. Today I have laid bare the foundations of the furnaces and cauldrons for you. Go now, gather wood and stone and shape your tools; the skill in your hands is made one pot at a time.

lore.meridian_brewing.metal_elixir:
Come, sit yourself down by this hearth-fire of mine. The night wind out in the swamp is damp and cold, seeping right into the marrow of your bones, so it is just the right time to toss a couple lumps of charcoal into the stove. What I am teaching you today is called White Alum Elixir. It is the metal medicine among the Five Elements elixirs, prepared especially for those impatient youngsters who cultivate metal methods. Back in my day, I saw plenty of sword cultivators running out of metal qi right when they crossed swords with their foes; who has the leisure to sit down and slowly breathe and meditate then? At times like that, tilting your head back to gulp down a bottle of White Alum Elixir sends that sharp metal qi surging straight into your already opened metal meridians on the spot. But you mark my words: this medicine is terribly fierce. It can only be kept in glass bottles and taken orally sip by sip, and by no means can it ever be made into a splash potion to be flung about.

The very first step of brewing medicine is to understand the fire and the stove. You must stand guard by the cauldron yourself, brewing it by hand without stepping away for a single moment. At the bottom, you need an iron brazier, and set a witch cauldron right on top of it. When an iron brazier is first placed down, it is cold, but it has Yang fire. If someone has swapped it to Yin fire, you can just grab a handful of sand and sprinkle it over to switch it back to Yang fire. Facing the cauldron, add charcoal or coal; adding fuel once raises it by 1 tier, and the furnace fire will burn steadily for 60 seconds. When we brew White Alum Elixir, the most vital thing about the temperature is keeping it pinned between 90–98 degrees. If you raise the iron brazier to level 3, the fire temperature sits right at 93 degrees, wavering up and down by only 1 degree, steady as can be. Setting a copper cauldron over a campfire can do in a pinch, but a campfire is Yang fire and its temperature always leaps around 100 degrees, which is far too hot. You would have to keep cold water bottles ready: pouring a bottle of cold water into a copper cauldron drops the temperature by 15 degrees, and by 10 degrees in a witch cauldron, and getting into a fluster can easily ruin everything.

Once the fire is going, it is time to prepare the ingredients. Other main ingredients are precious and demand meticulous processing, but the main ingredient for White Alum Elixir is not delicate in the least—it is just Iron Nuggets broken down from iron ingots. No processing required; just break iron ingots into Iron Nuggets and they can go straight into the pot. First, fill it to the brim with water: pouring from a water bucket adds 3 portions of water at a time, while pouring from a water bottle adds 1 portion at a time; a witch cauldron must be filled with 2 portions of water, while a copper cauldron takes 3 portions of water. Once it is full of water, toss the Iron Nugget in, and the recipe is set; right after that, put in the base ingredient, Glowstone Dust. Whatever you do, do not get itchy fingers and try stuffing gunpowder in there; this medicine is not permitted to become a splash potion, and gunpowder cannot be thrown into the cauldron. After putting in the base ingredient, do not rush to turn up the heat and start brewing. First let the temperature in the cauldron sit between 40–79 degrees, soaking gently for a full 10 seconds. Only when the ingredients have soaked up plenty of water will the brewed potency be pure.

When it comes time to begin the brew, you must first read this parchment recipe carefully, and then read the brewing scroll. Back in the day, I scavenged them deep in the swamp from the witch hut of an old witch in the True Qi realm; the parchment is not destroyed after reading, so just keep it in your head. With a stick in your right hand and your eyes fixed squarely on the cauldron, perform the brewing form, and this brewing lasts for a full 30 seconds. Hear an old woman's earnest warning: during these 30 seconds, your feet must never wander more than 3 blocks away from the cauldron, and your eyes must stay glued to the cauldron or the flames underneath it, unable to look away for even an instant. If you walk off or look elsewhere, this batch of medicine breaks right on the spot! But do not panic if it really does break; the ingredients and the time spent soaking are still resting at the bottom of the cauldron, so just take your stick and begin brewing anew. Starting the brew consumes true qi: a copper cauldron consumes 6 yuan of true qi, while a witch cauldron consumes 7.8 yuan, deducted evenly across the 30 seconds. It draws from the surrounding world first; if the world lacks enough, it deducts from your own meridians. If both combined are not enough, the brewing form simply will not start.

While brewing, timing when you add ingredients is the secret to the craft. Once brewing begins, when you reach seconds 6–10, pinch the secondary ingredient, Nether Quartz, in your left hand and toss it steadily into the cauldron. Then count patiently, and when you reach seconds 20–24, throw in the guide ingredient, a Gold Nugget, with your left hand. Missing the timing for adding ingredients by within 4 seconds either way is passable, but if you miss by more, the medicinal potency is completely wasted. Especially that Gold Nugget: if you do not throw it in, this batch will be Fine at best, and you will never brew a Superior one. While brewing, your eyes must also watch the heat: above 90 degrees, 1 portion of water will boil away every 20 seconds, so never let it boil dry. If the fire temperature is more than 8 degrees higher than 98 degrees, the medicine broth will scorch once every 3 seconds, and each scorch causes the quality to tumble down by a grade.

Once the full 30 seconds of brewing are done, the medicine broth will be rolling in the cauldron, but by no means should you ladle it out just yet! Haste makes waste, child; you must wait patiently for the cauldron temperature to cool down slowly, falling between 40–79 degrees, before taking empty glass bottles to scoop it up, one bottle per scoop. A witch cauldron yields exactly 1 bottle, and a copper cauldron yields 2 bottles. If you rush to ladle it out while it is scalding hot, the quality will be completely ruined at the very end.

When the elixir is done, its quality will show upon the bottle. If the heat was steady, the timing exact, the guide ingredient sufficient, and the ingredients followed the rules, what you ladle out will be Superior; slightly lesser batches will be Fine or Common, while clumsy craft turns it Poor; and if you botch it entirely, what you scoop up is merely a puddle of black dregs. Drinking this elixir pours true qi straight into those metal meridians you have already unblocked, like the Lung meridian and Large Intestine meridian. Poor yields 0.6 yuan of true qi, Common yields 1 yuan, Fine yields 1.5 yuan, and Superior reaches as high as 2.4 yuan. But remember, if you have not opened a single meridian belonging to metal, or if your meridians are already stuffed full of true qi, taking a swallow will simply scatter all that medicinal power into the world, wasted for nothing.

Lastly, this old woman must rap your knuckles with a ruler: fine as this White Alum Elixir is, its elixir toxin is terribly fierce! Metal qi is far too parched, and the moment you swallow a mouthful, your heart and lungs will feel as if roasted over a fire, leaving behind a layer of elixir toxin called Parched Lungs that will not disperse for a full 300 seconds, and not even chugging a bucket of milk will relieve it in the slightest. While carrying a layer of Parched Lungs, the true qi you draw in when closing your eyes to breathe and meditate is reduced to only 80% of what it usually is. If you get greedy and force down a second bottle before the Parched Lungs have cleared, the metal true qi granted by that second bottle is cut directly in half, the Parched Lungs on you worsen to a second layer, the true qi drawn from sitting and meditating drops to only 60%, and those 300 seconds start all over from the beginning! If you drink a third bottle, Parched Lungs stacks to a third layer, leaving your meditation at only 40%; and if you are reckless enough to drink a fourth bottle after that, you will receive not a single speck of true qi, purely suffering another 300 seconds of scorched heat in your chest for nothing. Luckily, the Five Elements elixirs each run through their own meridians, so carrying toxins left by other elixirs will not hinder you from drinking this one.

Do you understand now? This elixir is meant for emergencies, to gulp down a bottle right before battle to get yourself out of a tight spot. Once you drink it, rely honestly on your fists and weapons; do not expect to restore qi through meditation, and certainly do not blindly chug bottle after bottle. Off you go now: pick out the Iron Nuggets and Nether Quartz, and go light the iron brazier first to try your hand.
